question: The new Coastal Communities Strategy adopted by the Commission on 10 June is a welcome step towards protecting the EU’s 70 000 kilometres of coastline.

However, the western Black Sea region suffers from two vulnerabilities: firstly, severe coastal erosion exacerbated by specific hydrographic dynamics, and secondly, significant geopolitical and economic pressure on port infrastructure and communities close to the Danube Delta.

The Black Sea Member States, including Romania, are making major efforts to develop the offshore renewable (wind) energy sector, but face high costs of connecting and adapting critical coastal infrastructure. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that the funding mechanisms for the new strategy will reflect the characteristics and risks specific to the Black Sea basin, which has different dynamics from the Atlantic or Mediterranean basins?

What specific financial instruments will be made available from ‘blue carbon’ credits or innovation funds to help Black Sea ports to adapt infrastructure to accept offshore green energy and simultaneously combat erosion?

What specific measures does the strategy include for coastal communities in areas with special environmental protection regimes (such as the Danube Delta), where economic diversification is severely restricted by environmental regulations?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.8.2026) The EU Coastal Communities Strategy1 promotes a place-based approach to coastal development. It encourages Member States to use the flexibility of the future National and Regional Partnership Plans under the funding period 2028-2034, to address the strategy’s objectives and local needs, in cooperation with national, regional and local authorities.

The Common Maritime Agenda2 can support regional cooperation and provide a basin-level forum for regional actions specific to the Black Sea. The Communication on the EU’s eastern border regions3 set out an overarching plan for more secure, resilient and attractive places.

Future carbon farming activities in coastal ecosystems may be certified4 for CO2 removals thanks to the conservation, restoration, or management of these ecosystems, including by ports5. Any credits accrued may then be sold on the carbon market to offset emissions. The Commission is also working on a regulated nature credits market through the Roadmap towards Nature Credits.

6 The Strategy acknowledges that despite substantial protection efforts coastal and marine ecosystems remain under pressure, which risks undermining also the blue economy sectors. In areas under strict environmental protection regimes, economic resilience relies on diversifying towards low-impact activities.

The Commission highlights the diversification of sustainable blue economy models (including pesca-tourism), community initiatives, local value chains, blue bioeconomy clusters, nature-based solutions and co-management partnerships (including fishers) for protected areas as possible solutions. EU funding7 is available for biodiversity, climate resilience, sustainable water management and circular economy.
1 COM (2026) 530 final. 2 https://black-sea-maritime-agenda.ec.europa.eu/. 3 COM(2026) 82 final. 4 Under Regulation (EU) 2024/3012 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2024

establishing a Union certification framework for permanent carbon removals, carbon farming and carbon storage in products. 5 Such as mangrove forests, tidal marshes and seagrass meadows. 6 COM(2025) 374 final. The roadmap has a timeline for implementation until 2027. 7 Cohesion Policy funds, European Maritime, Fisheries, and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) and LIFE programme.
